summary: This Standards Track document augments the ietf-yang-library module from RFC 8525 with an augmented-by list. This makes it easier to find all dependencies between YANG modules by querying a server's YANG library. It updates RFC 8525.

questions: what is the yang library augmented-by list
how to find yang module augmentations
subtitle: A small YANG library extension that lists which modules augment which, so clients need not parse every module.

tldr.problem: The YANG library lists deviations but not augmentations, so a client wanting every reverse dependency of a module must fetch and parse all of a server's YANG modules.
tldr.mechanism: A new module, ietf-yang-library-augmentedby, adds an augmented-by leaf-list to each module entry, naming the modules that directly augment it within the same module-set.
tldr.outcome: Clients can read augmentation dependencies straight from the YANG library. The RFC updates RFC 8525.

today: RFC 10035 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026 that updates RFC 8525. The unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The YANG library of RFC 8525 is an inventory of the YANG modules a network management server supports. In YANG, an augment adds nodes to another module, and a deviation changes properties of another module's schema nodes. This RFC calls the resulting reliance on outside modules a reverse dependency.

The YANG library already has a deviation list, so a client can learn deviation dependencies without parsing every module. It has no equivalent for augmentations. This document adds one, and it updates RFC 8525 by extending the list in Section 2 of that RFC with the augmented-by list.

One requirement applies: a module and the modules that augment it MUST be listed in the same module-set, as already applies to deviations.
sections.eli5: The library already says who changes a chapter. This RFC makes it also say who adds to a chapter.

sections.title: Why Augmentations Need Listing
sections.content:
RFC 7950 identifies four kinds of dependency between YANG modules: import, include, augment and deviation. Import and include are direct dependencies visible in a module's own source. Augment and deviation are reverse dependencies defined in another module, so they cannot be discovered by parsing the module itself.

Today the way to find them is to query all YANG modules from the server and parse them. That is a lengthy process that every client needing the information must repeat. If the YANG library reported augmentations next to deviations, a client would have a much more convenient way to find all module dependencies.
sections.eli5: Some notes about a chapter are written in other chapters, not in the chapter itself. Without an index you have to read everything to find them.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The first use case is a data mesh architecture for YANG-Push telemetry. A receiver gets a notification for a subscription to ietf-interfaces, but the pushed data may also contain nodes from ietf-ip, which augments it. Today a receiver may fetch the whole set of modules from the device when a subscription starts. With the augmented-by information it can ask the server for the reverse dependencies of just the modules in the subscription, which saves collection and processing time.

The second is a data catalog. A catalog connector that reads the YANG library of a device would learn that it implements both ietf-interfaces and ietf-ip but would miss that one augments the other. The workaround is to fetch the modules and process them alongside the library data, which adds burden to the connector.
sections.eli5: A reader who gets a page full of notes needs to know which other pages those notes came from. The new list tells them straight away.

sections.title: The augmented-by Module
sections.content:
The new module ietf-yang-library-augmentedby (prefix yanglib-aug) augments ietf-yang-library with an augmented-by leaf-list on each module entry under yang-library/module-set. Each value is a leafref to the name of another module in the same module-set, and it lists the modules that directly augment the current one.

The same leaf-list is also added under the deprecated modules-state container, for servers that still use it for compatibility with RFC 7895. That copy is marked deprecated.

The entry MUST NOT refer, directly or indirectly, to the module being augmented, and MUST NOT be referenced in the import-only list. The same module can appear as an augmenter for several modules. Robust clients should handle a module that augments itself gracefully.
sections.eli5: Each chapter entry gets a small extra line that names the chapters that add to it.

sections.title: Direct Augmentation Only
sections.content:
The list only includes modules that directly augment the module in question. What counts is the module that owns the augmentation's target node, not the module at the start of the XPath. Recursive or schema-tree-specific dependency search is left to the application.

The RFC gives two examples with modules A, B and C in one module-set. In the first, B and C both augment /A:foo-a, so A lists both B and C. In the second, B augments /A:foo-a and C augments /A:foo-a/B:foo-b. Although C's XPath starts in A, the node it augments belongs to B, so A lists only B, and B lists C.
sections.eli5: If you scribble a note on a note someone else added to a chapter, your note is listed under that note, not under the chapter.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content: Base modules and their augmenting modules are required to be in the same module-set. The augmented-by data increases the size of the YANG library instance on the server. The library instance, and with it the augmented-by data, should be updated when new YANG modules are onboarded.
sections.eli5: A longer table of contents takes more room, and it has to be updated when new chapters are added.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines only read-only (config false) data nodes and no RPCs or actions. The nodes /yang-library/module-set/module/augmented-by and /modules-state/module/augmented-by may be sensitive in some networks, because they expose the augmentation relationships among modules on a server. Unauthorized read access could help an attacker identify the implementation structure or software components present, which might be used to target known platform vulnerabilities.

Access control policies SHOULD therefore restrict read access to authorized users, for example with NACM from RFC 8341. The security considerations of RFC 8525 also apply.
sections.eli5: A map showing how a building's parts connect could help a burglar, so only trusted people should be allowed to see it.
